results.title: Azure GPU Spot, Mapped: The August 2026 Report | Caleta.io Blog
results.author: John Holmes
highlights:
18 September 2026

# Azure GPU Spot, Mapped: The August 2026 Report

On 1 August, fifteen of the twenty-two deployable H100 regions cut spot by exactly 20.0%, the same move Azure made on 1 July. Then on 20 August something happened that had not happened in three months of daily snapshots: two regions changed price in the middle of the month, and both went up. We snapshot spot prices and eviction bands daily across ~1,500 SKU-region combinations. Here is the August picture for the five VMs you would actually run AI inference on, including the full tables.

...

## 1. The monthly reset held, for the third month running

Azure holds GPU spot prices flat for a calendar month and rewrites the list on the first. August delivered it again: fifteen regions cut by precisely 20.0% on 1 August, five did not move at all, and two moved by odd amounts (Germany West Central by 12.4%, East US by 8.1%). Both of the odd ones have the same explanation, covered in finding 3.

Three consecutive months of the same synchronised cut is no longer a curiosity. It is the shape of the product. If you are modelling Azure GPU spot as a live auction that responds to demand hour by hour, the data says otherwise.

...

On 20 August, mid-month, Malaysia West rose by exactly 10.0% and Central India by exactly 5.0%, on both H100 sizes. Nothing like it had appeared in June or July, where no tracked combination moved inside the month.

Malaysia West is worth watching because it was June's value pick: the cheapest H100 on the map at $1.5093, unchanged through July, and one of the calmest at a 0-5% band. It went to $1.6595 on 20 August, then to $1.8253 on 2 September. That is a 21% rise in two weeks for a region that had not moved in three months.

...

## 3. East US has fallen three months

...

East US has now cut its H100 spot price in three consecutive months:

| | June | July | August |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price | $1.7541 | $1.4030 | $1.2899 |
| Discount | 74.9% | 79.9% | 81.5% |
| Eviction band | 15%+ on 24 of 26 days | 0-5% all month | 0-5% all 31 days |

It is the cheapest H100 on the map and sits in Azure's lowest published eviction band on every single day of the month, which is the second month running that the cheap-means-risky rule does not hold.

...

The spread narrowed as a result. The same H100 hour costs $1.2899 in East US and $5.9634 in West US, a 4.6x spread, down from 5.3x in July.

...

## Appendix: the August H100 table

Single-GPU H100 (NC40ads), Linux, all 22 deployable regions. Prices are each month's modal value and eviction is the mean band midpoint over 31 August snapshots.

...

## Method

Prices come from the Azure Retail Prices API (Linux, Spot consumption meters), snapshotted daily. The August value shown is the month's modal price. Unlike June and July, August was not flat within the month: four tracked SKU-region combinations changed price on 20 August, all of them rises. Discount is calculated against the same region's pay-as-you-go price from the same API. Eviction comes from Azure's published eviction-rate band via Resource Graph, aggregated over 31 daily August snapshots at band midpoints. Regions priced in the API but absent from the Resource SKUs list, or never reporting an eviction band, are excluded as non-deployable: the same phantom-region screen as June and July, which excluded the same regions again.

...

Azure rewrites this price list on the first of each month, and in August it also rewrote part of it on the twentieth. September is already showing a less uniform reset than July or August did, which we will cover next month.

results.title: The bill is increasing even though prices haven't been raised | What is actually happening with AWS, Azure, and GCP｜梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
results.author: 梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
highlights:
“AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud have not raised prices yet.”

This is a sentence that always comes up when talking about cloud costs since the beginning of 2026. And it is half true. As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that the three companies have collectively raised the base prices for general-purpose compute or storage.

...

### There is certainly no sign of a blanket increase in base prices

I checked the AWS pricing page and What's New, Microsoft's licensing notices and Partner Center announcements, and the Google Cloud pricing change notification page. I went through them all, and as of September 2, 2026, there is no official announcement that base prices for general-purpose compute and storage are being raised across the board.

In response to an inquiry from DatacenterDynamics, AWS replied, “AWS's commitment to not raise pricing on fixed pricing models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged.” This is a statement that their policy of not raising prices for fixed-price models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged. The price revisions Microsoft made in 2026 were for Microsoft 365 (SaaS), which is a separate matter from the Azure infrastructure. What is listed on the Google Cloud “Infrastructure Services and Pricing Updates” page is still the content of the revisions implemented in October 2022 and April 2023.

...

### AWS GPU reservation slots have already gone up twice

However, it is not the case that there are no price increases at all.

AWS has a menu called EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, which allows you to reserve GPU computing resources for a set period. This pricing page states the following:

“Reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand for EC2 Capacity Blocks. The current prices are scheduled to be updated next in October, 2026.”

They are updated regularly based on supply and demand, with the next revision scheduled for October 2026. In other words, this menu is designed with the premise that prices will fluctuate.

In fact, it has moved twice since the beginning of 2026. In January, the p5e.48xlarge equipped with NVIDIA H200 was revised from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour in most regions, and the p5en.48xlarge was revised from $36.18 to $41.61. In July, after initially being announced for July 1 and then changed to July 7, the revisions covered P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de. The P6-B300 is at a level of $14.04 per hour per accelerator.

The prices for January mentioned here are only the amounts after the revision as of January. Because it went up again in July, the p5e.48xlarge currently on the pricing page is $47.76 per hour. That is exactly a 20 percent increase from $39.80.

AWS does not publish these revision rates. Since they do not keep old prices, the figures of “15 percent” and “20 percent” are calculated by news organizations and technical blogs that kept records of the price lists before and after the revisions. They are simply separate calculation results lined up, such as the January revision being exactly 15 percent and the July P5 revision being exactly 20 percent. It is not that AWS said “we are raising prices by 15 to 20 percent,” and the new and old prices themselves mentioned above are also based on the records of the reporting side.

...

### Azure

The FAQ regarding Microsoft Customer Agreements specifically describes how the rate is determined.

"We use London closing spot rates that are captured in the two business days prior to the last business day of the previous month end. (Omitted) This rate applies to all transactions during the upcoming month."

The London closing spot rate captured two business days before the last business day of the previous month is applied to all transactions in the following month. The same page even provides an example where the rate for January is determined in the final days of December and applied to all Azure purchases and consumption in January. Since the rate is fixed within the month, the impact of the weak yen appears in monthly steps.

...

- As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud have generally raised base prices for general-purpose compute and storage.
- However, prices have risen in specific areas. AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML were revised twice, in January and July 2026, and the pricing page states that the next revision is scheduled for October 2026. AWS has not disclosed the revision rate, and the "15 to 20 percent" figure circulating is a value back-calculated from the old and new prices.
- Google Cloud raised prices for egress via CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering starting May 1, 2026. In North America, the price doubled from $0.04 to $0.08 per GiB. Cloud CDN itself and general egress are not affected.
- For all three companies, the structure in Japan is that list prices are in dollars, while billing is in yen. Azure determines the rate based on the London closing price two business days before the end of the previous month, Google Cloud at the beginning of each month, and AWS at the time the invoice is created. The Japanese yen is not included in Google Cloud's currency fluctuation protection target currencies.
- Therefore, even if the provider does not raise prices, the billed amount will increase if the yen weakens. The standard foreign exchange rate has gone from 145 yen in July 2025 to 163 yen for the September 2026 application period.
- Domestically, Fujitsu will implement price revisions for FJcloud-V and others on October 1, 2026. The revision rates have not been publicly disclosed to that extent.
- In the State of FinOps 2026, 98 percent of organizations responded that they are managing AI spending (up from 31 percent two years ago), and SaaS spending management has reached 90 percent.

results.title: What It Actually Costs to Rent an H100, H200, or B200 in September 2026
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
- As of early September 2026, on-demand H100 rental still runs about $2–4/GPU-hr on specialty clouds (Vast.ai floor ~$1.49, GMI ~$2.00, Spheron ~$2.01, RunPod ~$2.69, Lambda ~$3.99) versus a ~$10–13/hr median on AWS/Azure/GCP/Oracle — a 5–6× spread for the identical card, essentially unchanged from August.
- H200 held or softened slightly: ~$2.30–2.60/hr at the floor (FluidStack ~$2.30, GMI ~$2.60), up to ~$6.31 at CoreWeave, with Nebius easing to ~$4.50.
- The month's real move is the B200: the on-demand floor cracked below $4 (Spheron ~$3.70, Packet.ai ~$3.75, GMI ~$4.00, down from August's ~$4.99), spot near $2.12–2.74, and the provider field widened to 30+. Grace-Blackwell GB200 superchips also started renting by the hour (GMI from ~$8.00, Oracle ~$16).
- The twist: while neoclouds cut, AWS RAISED its H200 capacity-block prices 15% on Jan 4, 2026 (p5e.48xlarge $34.61→$39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades.
- The decision is still utilization, not sticker: a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it's busy or not, and below roughly 40–50% duty cycle a per-token API almost always beats renting metal.

- H200 (141GB) — more memory, held or softened. About $2.30–6.31/hr on-demand: ~$2.30 at the FluidStack floor, ~$2.60 at GMI, ~$4.50 at Nebius (down from ~$5.50 in August), ~$6.31 at CoreWeave. Note a hyperscaler quirk: AWS's H200 via capacity blocks (~$4.98/GPU) is actually cheaper than its own H100 on-demand list rate, while Azure's H200 sits at the top of the range (~$10.60–13.78).
- B200 (Blackwell) — the month's real move. The on-demand floor cracked below $4: ~$3.70 at Spheron, ~$3.75 at Packet.ai (the cheapest in-stock rate GetDeploying tracked on Sept 3), ~$4.00 at GMI — down from August's ~$4.99 floor — with spot near $2.12–2.74 and the provider field widened to 30+.
